summary: Describes two ways to encapsulate multiprotocol network traffic over AAL5 on ATM networks. It replaced RFC 1483.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM networks move traffic in fixed-size cells, so ordinary packets have to be cut up and put back together. This document defines two ways to carry those packets: either each packet carries a header naming its protocol, or each ATM connection is set aside for one protocol. It gives the exact bytes for both.

questions: how is ip carried over atm
subtitle: Two ways to carry ordinary packets over an ATM network, with or without a per-packet header.

tldr.problem: ATM networks carry traffic in fixed 53-octet cells, but hosts, routers and bridges need to send variable-length packets of many protocols over them, and the receiver must know which protocol each packet carries.
tldr.mechanism: Packets are placed in the payload of an AAL5 CPCS-PDU. Either an LLC header, plus a SNAP header where needed, goes in front of each packet to name its protocol, which allows many protocols on one virtual connection, or each virtual connection is dedicated to one protocol and carries no header.
tldr.outcome: This memo replaced RFC 1483, added a VPN identification header and security considerations, and is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: LLC header fields
facts.value: DSAP, SSAP and Ctrl, one octet each

today: RFC 2684 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1999. It obsoletes RFC 1483 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the definition of multiprotocol encapsulation over ATM Adaptation Layer type 5.

sections.title: Two Ways to Carry Traffic over ATM
sections.content:
Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) wide area, campus and local area networks carry IP datagrams and other connectionless traffic between hosts, routers, bridges and other networking devices. This document describes two methods for carrying connectionless routed and bridged Protocol Data Units (PDUs) over an ATM network.

The LLC Encapsulation method allows multiplexing of multiple protocols over a single ATM virtual connection. The protocol type of each PDU is identified by a prefixed IEEE 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) header. In the VC Multiplexing method, each ATM virtual connection carries PDUs of exactly one protocol type, and there is a separate VC for each protocol.

The unit of transport in ATM is a 53 octet fixed length PDU called a cell. A cell consists of a 5 octet header and a 48 byte payload. Variable length PDUs must be segmented by the transmitter to fit into the 48 octet cell payload and reassembled by the receiver. This document specifies the ATM Adaptation Layer type 5 (AAL5) for this purpose, and variable length PDUs are carried in the Payload field of the AAL5 Common Part Convergence Sublayer (CPCS) PDU.

The document applies to implementations that use ATM networks to carry multiprotocol traffic among hosts, routers and bridges that are ATM end systems. It describes only how routed and bridged PDUs are carried directly over the AAL5 CPCS, that is, when the Service Specific Convergence Sublayer is absent. If the Frame Relay SSCS is used over the CPCS, routed and bridged PDUs are carried using the NLPID multiplexing method of RFC 2427, which MUST be used in the special case of Frame Relay Network Interworking or transparent mode Service Interworking. If the facilities designed for the Point-to-Point Protocol are wanted and a point-to-point relationship exists between peer systems, then RFC 2364 applies instead of this document.

The choice between the two methods depends on implementation and system requirements. In general, LLC encapsulation tends to require fewer VCs in a multiprotocol environment, while VC multiplexing tends to reduce fragmentation overhead. When two ATM end systems exchange connectionless PDUs across an ATM Permanent Virtual Connection, the method is chosen by configuration. ATM connection control signalling procedures are used to negotiate the encapsulation method when ATM Switched Virtual Connections are used.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM networks move traffic in fixed-size cells. To send an ordinary packet over one, the sender cuts it up and the receiver puts it back together. This document defines the two ways that can be done.

sections.title: The AAL5 CPCS-PDU Format
sections.content:
For both multiplexing methods, routed and bridged PDUs MUST be encapsulated within the Payload field of an AAL5 CPCS-PDU. The AAL5 message mode service, in the non-assured mode of operation, MUST be used. The corrupted delivery option MUST NOT be used, and a reassembly timer MAY be used.

The CPCS-PDU holds a Payload field of up to 2^16 - 1 octets of user information, a PAD field of 0 to 47 octets, and a trailer of four fields. The PAD field pads the CPCS-PDU so that it fits exactly into the ATM cells, with the trailer right justified in the last 48 octet cell payload created by the SAR sublayer.

The trailer holds the CPCS-UU (User-to-User indication) field of one octet, which is not used by the multiprotocol ATM encapsulation described here and MAY be set to any value. The CPI (Common Part Indicator) field of one octet aligns the trailer to 64 bits and MUST be coded as 0x00. The Length field of two octets gives the length, in octets, of the Payload field; the maximum value is 65535, and a Length field coded as 0x00 is used for the abort function. The CRC field of four octets uses a CRC-32 to detect bit errors in the CPCS-PDU.
sections.plainLanguage: Both methods put the packet inside an AAL5 container. The container has a payload area for the packet, some padding so the last cell lines up, and a trailer that holds the payload length and a checksum.

sections.title: LLC Encapsulation for Routed Protocols
sections.content:
In LLC Encapsulation, the protocol type of routed PDUs MUST be identified by prefixing an IEEE 802.2 LLC header to each PDU. In some cases the LLC header MUST be followed by an IEEE 802.1a SubNetwork Attachment Point (SNAP) header. In LLC Type 1 operation the LLC header MUST consist of three one octet fields, DSAP, SSAP and Ctrl, and the Ctrl field MUST be set to 0x03, specifying an Unnumbered Information command PDU.

The LLC header value 0xFE-FE-03 identifies a routed PDU in the ISO NLPID format. For such a PDU the Payload field holds the LLC header, then an NLPID field of one octet, then the PDU, up to 2^16 - 4 octets. The NLPID values are administered by ISO and ITU-T and are defined in ISO/IEC TR 9577. An NLPID value of 0x00 is the Null Network Layer or Inactive Set and, since it has no significance in this context, MUST NOT be used.

Although there is an NLPID value of 0xCC that indicates IP, the NLPID format MUST NOT be used for IP. IP datagrams MUST be identified by a SNAP header instead. The presence of a SNAP header is indicated by the LLC header value 0xAA-AA-03. A SNAP header consists of a three octet Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) and a two octet Protocol Identifier (PID). The OUI is administered by IEEE and identifies the organization that administers the values assigned to the PID, so the two together identify the protocol uniquely. The OUI value 0x00-00-00 indicates that the PID is an EtherType.

For an IPv4 PDU the EtherType value is 0x08-00, and the payload holds the LLC header, the OUI, the EtherType and the IPv4 PDU, up to 2^16 - 9 octets. This format is consistent with the one defined in RFC 1042.
sections.plainLanguage: When one connection carries several kinds of packet, each packet must say what it is. A Logical Link Control header of three one octet fields comes first, then either a one octet NLPID field or a SNAP header made of a three octet OUI and a two octet PID. IPv4 always uses the SNAP form, with the EtherType 0x08-00.

sections.title: LLC Encapsulation for Bridged Protocols
sections.content:
In LLC Encapsulation, bridged PDUs are encapsulated by identifying the type of the bridged media in the SNAP header. The presence of the SNAP header MUST be indicated by the LLC header value 0xAA-AA-03, and the OUI value MUST be the 802.1 organization code 0x00-80-C2. The two octet PID specifies the type of the bridged media and also indicates whether the original Frame Check Sequence (FCS) is preserved within the bridged PDU.

The necessary number of padding octets MUST be added after the PID field to align the Ethernet/802.3 LLC Data field, the 802.4 Data Unit field, the 802.5 Info field, the FDDI Info field or the 802.6 Info field of the bridged PDU to begin at a four octet boundary. The bit ordering of the MAC address MUST be the same as it would be on the LAN or MAN.

Because the Ethernet/802.3 physical layer requires frames to be padded to a minimum size, a bridge that uses the Bridged Ethernet/802.3 format with the preserved LAN FCS MUST include padding. A bridge that uses that format without the preserved LAN FCS MAY either include padding or omit it. A bridge that receives a frame in this format without the LAN FCS MUST be able to insert the necessary padding, if none is already present, before forwarding to an Ethernet/802.3 subnetwork.

Each bridged media type has its own PID values and its own padding length. Ethernet/802.3 uses PID 0x00-01 or 0x00-07 with two padding octets, 802.4 uses PID 0x00-02 or 0x00-08 with three padding octets, 802.5 uses PID 0x00-03 or 0x00-09 with three padding octets of which the last may be any value, FDDI uses PID 0x00-04 or 0x00-0A with three padding octets, and 802.6 uses PID 0x00-0B. Bridge Protocol Data Units use PID 0x00-0E.

The 802.6 format also carries a Common PDU Header and Trailer, so that the egress bridge can start transmitting segments of a segmented PDU before it has received the whole thing. An ingress 802.6 bridge can abort an AAL5 CPCS-PDU by setting its Length field to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Bridged packets, which carry frames from an Ethernet or token ring network, are marked with the type of the media they came from. The PID value also says whether the frame's checksum is still there.

sections.title: VC Multiplexing
sections.content:
VC Multiplexing creates a binding between an ATM VC and the type of the network protocol carried on that VC. There is then no need for protocol identification information in the payload of each AAL5 CPCS-PDU. This reduces payload overhead and can reduce per-packet processing. VC multiplexing can improve efficiency by reducing the number of cells needed to carry PDUs of certain lengths.

For ATM PVCs, the type of the protocol to be carried over each PVC MUST be determined by configuration. For ATM SVCs, the negotiation specified in RFC 1755 MUST be used. Routed PDUs MUST be carried as the only content of the Payload of the AAL5 CPCS-PDU, up to 2^16 - 1 octets. Bridged PDUs MUST be carried in the Payload as described in Section 5.2, except that only the fields after the PID field MUST be included, because the virtual connection already carries the media type.

For Ethernet, 802.3, 802.4, 802.5 and FDDI PDUs, the presence or absence of the trailing LAN FCS is identified implicitly by the VC, since the PID field is not included. PDUs with the LAN FCS and PDUs without the LAN FCS are thus considered to belong to different protocols, even if the bridged media type would be the same.
sections.plainLanguage: The other method binds one ATM connection to one protocol. Then no per-packet header is needed, which saves bytes and processing. The receiver is told which protocol the connection carries by configuration or by the signalling that sets the connection up.

sections.title: Bridging in an ATM Network
sections.content:
A bridge with an ATM interface that serves as a link to one or more other bridges MUST be able to flood, forward and filter bridged PDUs. Flooding is performed by sending the PDU to all possible appropriate destinations, which in the ATM environment means sending the PDU through each relevant VC. This may be done by explicitly copying it to each VC or by using a point-to-multipoint VC.

To forward a PDU, a bridge MUST be able to associate a destination MAC address with a VC. It is unreasonable, and perhaps impossible, to require bridges to configure statically an association of every possible destination MAC address with a VC. ATM bridges must therefore provide enough information to allow an ATM interface to learn dynamically about foreign destinations beyond the set of ATM stations.

To accomplish dynamic learning, a bridged PDU MUST conform to the encapsulation described in Section 5. In this way the receiving ATM interface knows to look into the bridged PDU and learn the association between the foreign destination and an ATM station.
sections.plainLanguage: A bridge that connects to other bridges over ATM has to flood unknown frames, forward known ones and drop the rest. It learns which connection reaches which destination by reading the frames it receives.

sections.title: Identifying a VPN
sections.content:
The encapsulation defined in this section applies only to Virtual Private Networks that operate over an ATM subnet. A mechanism for globally unique identification of Virtual Private multiprotocol networks is defined in RFC 2685. The 7-octet VPN-Id consists of a 3-octet VPN-related OUI, followed by a 4-octet VPN index that is allocated by the owner of the VPN-related OUI. Typically the VPN-related OUI value is assigned to a VPN service provider, which then allocates VPN index values for its customers.

The VPN encapsulation header is the LLC header 0xAA-AA-03, the OUI 0x00-00-5E, the PID 0x00-08, a pad octet, the 3-octet VPN-related OUI and the 4-octet VPN index. When the encapsulation header is used, the remainder of the PDU MUST be structured according to the appropriate format described in Section 5 or Section 6, that is, the VPN encapsulation header is prepended to the PDU within an AAL5 CPCS SDU.

For a routed or bridged PDU sent within a VPN using LLC encapsulation, the VPN encapsulation header MUST be prepended to the appropriate format defined in Sections 5.1 and 5.2. For VC multiplexing, the VPN identifier MAY instead be specified a priori, using ATM connection control signalling or an administrative assignment to an ATM interface. If the VPN is identified that way, all PDUs carried by the VC, or by any VC within the interface, are associated with the same VPN and the payload formats are those of Sections 6.1 and 6.2. If a PDU is received containing a VPN encapsulation header when the VPN has been identified another way, the receiver MAY drop it and take other implementation-specific actions. If the identifier is to be indicated using an encapsulation header, then that header MUST be prepended to the formats of Sections 6.1 and 6.2.
sections.plainLanguage: A virtual private network gets a seven octet identifier, made of an organization code and a four octet number. When the identifier is carried in the packet, a small header with that code is put in front of the payload.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This memo defines mechanisms for multiprotocol encapsulation over ATM. There is an element of trust in any encapsulation protocol: a receiver must trust that the sender has correctly identified the protocol being encapsulated. There is no way to ascertain that the sender did use the proper protocol identification, and it would not be desirable functionality. The encapsulation mechanisms described here are believed to have no other properties that might be exploited by an attacker. Architectures and protocols operating above the encapsulation layer may, however, be subject to a variety of attacks. In particular, the bridging architecture discussed in Section 7 has the same vulnerabilities as other bridging architectures.

System security may also be affected by the properties of the underlying ATM network. The ATM Forum has published a security framework and a security specification, which may be relevant.
sections.plainLanguage: Any encapsulation scheme needs trust: the receiver cannot check that the sender labelled the protocol correctly. Nothing else in this scheme looks exploitable, but the bridging rules above have the same weaknesses as any bridge.
